utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we're having problems with my laptop. I am not receiving -- the text is not scrolling on my -- let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Now it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but over here. But here it isn't in my notebook. So in the meantime, we can start, and I'll ask one of the technicians, if possible, to come over and try and solve this problem for me. It's only mine. Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could I ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam, and good afternoon. Appearances. Mr. Oric, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour; ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, and good afternoon for the Defence team as well. I'm here together with co-counsel, Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to, Mr. Wubben, and your team, of course. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is John Jones, and I appear on behalf of Naser Oric, with Jasmina Cosic and Geoff Roberts, our legal assistant and CaseMap manager respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you and your team. I see you are not the full team today. Do I assume that we are in the same position as we left it last time that, in other words, Madam Vidovic is back here, or will be back here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: She won't be back today. She'll be back towards the end of this week. In fact, I think probably on Sunday. But that doesn't prevent us from continuing. We're in a position deal with witnesses this week and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important thing. In the meantime, please convey to Madam Vidovic our best wishes for a quick recovery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I will do. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this week, the Prosecution tried to reschedule the witnesses, and we filed subsequently our projected witnesses list as such. And another issue is that we hand over today a courtesy copy of a videolink conference motion that's due after Easter, meaning that the day after Easter, we request the Trial Chamber to have the videolink conference with one of our projected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The day after Easter, that would be when?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The 29th and 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we will be here. We will not be here. We are going to have an Easter recess, starting from Thursday the 24th, resuming Monday, the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Oh, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also because of certain needs that some of us have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, we will withdraw our motion and refile it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, you refile it with another day. But In fact, I was coming back to you on this, that according to the list of witnesses that I had, it seemed that you had intended to bring a witness -- to have a witness here on the 24th, which is Thursday. Yes, exactly. On the 24th, we won't be able to sit. We'll sit until the 23rd. We'll sit until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We'll take that into account and reschedule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio has another application to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, delegated problems. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, can I just address you in private session about this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Di Fazio. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Witness, the proceedings will proceed -- will continue with your testimony being given in open session. One moment. I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation. Just give me a sign with your head. Yes, okay, don't speak for the time being, please. So the -- your testimony will proceed now in private session. However -- in public session. However, after hearing your request for protective measures, and after having heard also the Prosecution and the Defence in this regard, we have come to the conclusion to grant you the following protective measures; namely, that you will testify with voice and facial distortion, and of course under a pseudonym, because otherwise the rest wouldn't make sense. So you are going to be referred to as Witness C008. And I enjoin both parties to please remember that when addressing the witness, not to address her by her own name. That's number 1. Number 2 is the following: We will be, as I said, having voice distortion in place. That entails some caution on each and every one present here in this courtroom, in the sense that when the witness is speaking, then all other microphones must be switched off, so I take it that if, for example, you, Mr. Di Fazio, have just put a question to the witness, before she starts answering your question, please switch off your microphone. It's impossible for me to keep track and watch each and every one of you continuously while I also have to watch the witness, her demeanour, monitor the transcript, and everything. So please try to cooperate with us as much as you can. We will, at the same time, try to pay as much attention to these matters as much as we can, but please try to do the same yourselves. So, Witness C008, we are now going to proceed with your testimony, start, actually, with your testimony. I hope you have understood what I said before, and that you are happy with the protective measures that we have granted you. Mr. Di Fazio will be the first one to go. After all, you have been summoned to give testimony here by the Office of the Prosecutor. The procedure is, as it is in any other court of law, where you will be asked a question, you are required to answer that question. I suggest to you that not only you're bound by the solemn declaration that you entered earlier, but I suggest to you also that you try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question; otherwise, you will be here for ages. The same applies later on. After Mr. Di Fazio has concluded his examination-in-chief, then it will be Mr. Jones, who is appearing for Mr. Oric, who will cross-examine you. You owe him the same honesty and truthfulness in your own answers as you do when asked questions by the Prosecution. You have no right to distinguish between Prosecution and Defence. Your duty is to answer all questions truthfully and fully, to the best of your ability, irrespective of who is putting them to you. Again, when you are answering the questions put to you by Mr. Jones, please try to be brief and answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. I leave you now in the hands of Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Di Fazio, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask the witness now, in the period relevant to the indictment, what was her occupation, whether, in particular, she was employed in any particular office that you intend to ask her questions about. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is important for the purposes of -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've given a description of the various acronyms used as a result of name changes of this organisation that you worked for. In 1992 and 1993, were you working in just such an organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What name did it bear in 1992 and 1993? MR. DI FAZIO: The witness seems to have trouble with her headphones, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please switch off your microphone, please. Are you receiving interpretation? At the moment there are problems with the interpretations, please raise your hand and draw our attention straight away, please. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you answer Mr. Di Fazio's question now? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll repeat it, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were working in 1992 and 1993. What I want you to tell the Trial Chamber is this: What was the name of the organisation that you were working for in 1992 and 1993? Which of those various acronyms did it bear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, it was called the Office of State Security, and in 1993, it was the Agency for Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the name changes, was there any significant difference in your job and the responsibilities that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not in dispute that you were responsible for the intercepts of telephone conversations in the sense that you would transcribe intercepted telephone calls. And I want to ask you now to -- about that. Firstly, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the method of recording intercepted telephone calls was in your section in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please explain in more detail what actually you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was there a method of recording telephone conversations that you adopted in 1992 and 1993, using cassette tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me as an employee, the method was not known, so I would get a cassette, I would take it off, put it into the player, and then I would transcribe the conversation recorded on that tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that part of the process in due course, but I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber of the methodology used before that. How was the actual recording first made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The recording was made at the switchboard, so there was a switchboard which was -- which was recording. This method was not available to me as an employee. My part of work was to transcribe this tape, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that fully. I understand that fully. But what I'm asking you about is the creation of the tape in the first place. First of all, were cassette tapes used? Just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would -- how would the cassette tape be used in order to record a conversation on a telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A tape, a cassette, was put into the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the targeted telephone was being used, what would this switchboard machine do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when somebody started to talk, if this was the person that -- whose telephone calls we were intercepting, then at the time when that person phoned somebody, or when somebody would phone him, immediately the switchboard would switch on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that when the recording would be made on the cassette tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That recording would automatically be left on the tape, so the recording was on the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. So at the end of the conversation, when the phone is no longer being used, would the cassette keep recording or would it terminate the recording process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cassette could be of 60 or 90 minutes of length, depending on the need. If we wanted to make the job as quick as possible, we would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. immediately take the tape off and transcribe the tape, or we would leave it there to record several phone conversations on the same tape. So you could keep it running for the full length of 90 minutes or 60 minutes, depending on the kind of tape used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer to be, therefore, that one cassette tape might contain several intercepted -- sorry, might contain recordings of several intercepted telephone conversations on the same phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the process of initiating the recording and termination of the recording on the cassette automatic? In other words, was it performed by the machine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a system of lights on this machine that conducted the recording of the telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did lights on the machine indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the light was turned on, it meant that the conversation started, and if the light was turned off, it meant that the conversation was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we leave this topic, one more matter. Well, I'll withdraw that. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, about now is time for our break, if this is an opportune moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a break. Try to keep it as short as possible. MR. DI FAZIO: As you can see, I'm going to be very fast this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, let's proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hardly answer that question. What I receive is a proposal saying that a measure has been taken against a certain telephone. It is not up to me to decide who will be tapped, or why. What I do is I receive a proposal and I take the conversation down from the phone that has been requested. That's when my job stops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the time that you were working there in 1992 and 1993, did you hear the same person -- often hear the same person using a particular intercepted telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to identify that person, as time went by, as a result of the person saying who he or she was over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back to 1992 and 1993, did you also come to recognise particular voices used on particular telephones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If, for example, I were given a transcript to listen to again, I'm sure I would very soon identify the speaker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean, do I understand you to say, therefore, that back in 1992 and 1993, after having heard telephone conversations involving a particular speaker, you were able to recognise that person's voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After, perhaps, 10 or 15 days, I would be certain about who's speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would be in a position to identify a speaker during a telephone conversation not only as a result of the person saying who he or she was but also because you recognised voices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The system of transcription now. You've told us about the system of recording. I'd like you now to explain to the Trial Chamber the system of transcription that you've referred to. What did you do once an intercepted call had been recorded on these cassettes that you have mentioned? MR. DI FAZIO: I saw the witness gesticulating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear my last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once a cassette was taken off the switchboard's reel, you would put it on a different reel-to-reel recorder. You'd switch it on and you'd go from conversation to conversation. Everything that has been recorded is faithfully transcribed by your own hand. This wasn't something that was typewritten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that your job in 1993 and 1992, to listen to these tapes and transcribe the contents in your own handwriting onto paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed, because, I mean, these things have been circulating in my mind for quite some time, actually, because of course I cannot anticipate what your questions are. Has the witness been given clearance by the organisation she works for to come and testify here? That's question number 1. The reason, Mr. Di Fazio, I think I know a little bit about these things, as much as you and Mr. Jones do, I mean, members of the security agencies of countries do not just fall down from heaven and turn into prosecution witnesses in court cases just like that. I mean, they obtain clearance first, security clearance. MR. DI FAZIO: Do Your Honours have the witness' statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm suggesting this: It's because I would like you to put the question. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Amir Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is his position Minister Councillor, Liaison Officer, with the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June of 2004, did he grant permission to you to discuss the sorts of matters that I've been asking you about, to provide that information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through my service. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that's as far as I can go. Does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is necessary, because whoever is following the proceedings outside -- outside this Tribunal, particularly in Yugoslavia, ought to know that this witness particularly did not knock at the door of the Office of the Prosecutor and say, Can I please give you information on intercepts, et cetera. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number 1. The second thing that I would like the witness to inform the Trial Chamber about is who decided on who would be -- would have his telephone line bugged, and what would someone in the position of the witness, in the chain of -- know at that point in time. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'll ask the witness that, if Your Honours please. I don't know how much information we'll get, but I'll ask her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question of targeting of individuals, and the recording of their telephone conversations and the subsequent transcription, were you in any way concerned with that process; namely, the selection of persons whose phone calls were going to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the persons whose conversations you transcribed, did you know why they were being -- their conversations were being recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We would simply receive a request, a proposal, saying that such and such phone lines should be tapped for security reasons, and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Would the information be -- or the instructions refer only to a particular telephone, or would you also have an indication as to who owns that telephone line, or to whom that telephone line belongs? And in that case, would you be told the name of that person or would that person be referred to by a pseudonym or a code name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes I would get the name and sometimes I would get a pseudonym. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown P354. Your Honours, the English version of this document is on Sanction. And, of course, if the witness could be shown the B/C/S version of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to see the B/C/S version of this transcript as well, at least for a while, just to have a glance at it. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps it can be put on the ELMO, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, it's all right. I don't need to see it anymore. It's important that the witness sees it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until you finish this initial part, I don't think it's in the public interest to know which department she was in. MR. DI FAZIO: That is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the operative numbers and whatever. I think we can keep that in private session, and we'll take it up from there, after you've finished with that part. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I can return to it later in my examination-in-chief. I think that's probably the way to deal with it, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm just trying to be helpful and also not to go beyond what is acceptable practice in certain areas. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take you down to the last notation that occurs in P354, at the top left-hand corner. There's a number there. Do you see that number, 7335/256? My question is this: What does the number 7335 represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the number of the cassette that was taken off the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's another number there that appears, the number 256, following that number. Did you write that number? If you didn't, do you know what it means? And if you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is no, you did not write it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not having written it, can you tell us what it means? If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be some sort of a file number, once it was written down. And it probably was sent to be part of some file or other, but I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just continue down the page to the next line. There's a reference to Zolja and Z2. Please explain to Their Honours what that means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zolja is a code name for a phone line. Zolja simply means phone, and the word used here is Zolja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Z2, is that a reference to a particular telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that this phone was at switchboard 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next line says that the Zolja, the telephone, was being used by an entity or someone or something referred to as Skup. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a pseudonym for a facility, a feature, under inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In simple terms, is that a reference to a telephone, or a particular telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where that particular telephone was located back in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere at the command. It was a telephone at the Bosnia-Herzegovina army headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thinking back to 1992 and 1993, did a number of different individuals have access to that particular telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next notation is self-explanatory, I suppose. I assume it means that the telephone conversation itself that is then recorded occurred on the 11th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next notation, "reported on the 11th of February, 1993," what does that mean, "reported"? What precisely does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that the conversation was written up on the same day it was heard on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next line, again, says "Zeljko called Sefer" and they had the following conversation. Do you know who the Sefer is that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Zeljko? Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't get the witness' answer. MR. DI FAZIO: I heard no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So did I. I heard the witness say no. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, I'm grateful to you for that indulgence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there then appears a further notation, "Counter number: 037." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that the number on the counter of the reel-to-reel recorder was 037. This may be preceded by a blank tape or a conversation that didn't matter. This is just for those who were transcribing the various conversations, to be able to locate them on a given tape more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the "S," does it refer to the words of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the "Z," does it does it refer to the words of the man called Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P355.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go through this document a little faster. We've seen various notations in the previous document, P354. Again, in this document, P355, there is a number, 7644, followed by the number 385. Again, is that the number of the tape and the number of -- sorry, is that the number of the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, is the number 385 a number that was written there by someone other than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, there is a reference in that document to a man called Sefer. In that transcription, is the "S" a reference to Sefer, Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, there's reference to counter numbers. Does your previous explanation also apply to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, most importantly, whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. This time we also find on the first page another name now, Hazim. Is that a name or a code name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you know who that Hazim is or was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P356.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Witness, that I can save some time. Does all of the evidence that you've given thus far regarding P354 and P355 apply to this document in the sense that the numbers of the cassettes are seen, the date of transcription is seen, the date of conversation is seen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a reference to Sefer. Is that a reference to Sefer Halilovic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a reference to the other speaker, Rasim. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the "S" in the transcription a reference to the recording of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it your handwriting in that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, we see the reference to counter numbers. Does the explanation that you provided previously also apply to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P360.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you just cast your eye -- THE USHER: Just a moment. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just cast your eye, Witness, over the features of this document, P360, which has many features in common with the preceding documents I've shown you. Again, you see a number, 7299. Is that the cassette number -- cassette number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular document, there is a reference to someone called Sadic, calling Zicro Suljevic. Do you know who Sadic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Zicro Suljevic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Counter numbers appear here. Again, does the same explanation that you previously gave apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can we go into private session briefly -- closed session briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Before we go into closed or private session for a while, Judge Eser would like to put a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness, if you take the last document, your own transcription, am I right, is -- where you start "How are you," from there on, that's your transcription of this. Now, the line before, "Sadic calling Zicro Suljevic and they had the following conversation," that was something which -- a statement made by you in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the terminology that we used to apply, so it -- before the beginning of the conversation, we would always write that person called that person, and from there on it was their conversation. This was the terminology of our department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Sadic calling Zicro Suljevic," how did you know that the conversation was conducted between these two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they introduced one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard you say in the same sentence that you wanted private session and closed session, so could I ask you what your preference is, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I think private session will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm prepared to go into closed session for a while, if it's something which -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours. It's just a few minor matters about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session for a while then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing, following on from Judge Eser's question, you told us that you knew who the persons were participating in conversations from other information. If there was ever any doubt in your mind, as the transcriber, as to the identity of a caller or a speaker during a telephone conversation, would you reflect that doubt in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In case that I did not know who that was, I would write down, "Person X." If there were two persons whose identity I was not aware of, then I would say that it was an X person talking to an XY person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jones, I suppose -- I take it that you are prepared already?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. If Your Honour would give me one moment just to move over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's always a slight technical hitch, but I'm told it's better if it's raised. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I have a few questions for you, and I want to start by asking you some questions to set the scene in the state of communications as they were in Sarajevo during the siege. And I'm asking you that as someone who lived through the siege of Sarajevo and as someone whose work involved telephones. Just so that's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you maybe clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that wasn't a question, that was just a preface. Now, a very obvious question, firstly: Sarajevo was encircled and under siege from 1992 to 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, within Sarajevo, there were phone lines, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that those phone lines would go to what you've called a central, a telephone exchange, which would be located in the post office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question. I can only answer the questions related to my own work, my own profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. It's to understand, in fact, how it came about that your department had access to these telephone conversations. So isn't it correct that, in fact, there was a line, or there were lines, cable, going from the main telephone exchange to the SDB office, and that's where you would pick up the telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were receiving telephone calls in our building. In which way, I really cannot say. There were people whose task it was to provide that. I don't know how they did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. I want to just explore just a couple of hypotheticals for telephone conversations during the war, and I want to take the example, firstly, of someone in Sarajevo trying to phone someone in Tuzla. Now, there are no telephone -- there were no telephone lines going from Sarajevo to Tuzla, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a certain period of time, there were; in a certain period of time, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm referring to physical telephone lines as opposed to some other connection. Isn't it correct that, certainly in 1992 and 1993, there weren't physical telephone lines, telephone poles, going from Sarajevo to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were phone lines, because we had these phone conversations. In which way they were established, I really can't explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, if you're aware, isn't it -- isn't it right that, for a phone call to be relayed at that time from Sarajevo to Tuzla, it would actually have to be sent via radio transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In certain cases, that was true. But we also had examples of phone calls from Sarajevo to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or from Sarajevo to some other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now, if you're aware, either from personal experience or from your work, are you aware that the Serbs had receivers with which they could listen into different frequencies and intercept phone calls between Sarajevo and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time - and when I don't specify a time, I'm speaking about 1992/1993 - there were concerns on the Bosnian side that communications, telephone communications, were open; they could be listened into by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you also aware that Serbs could intercept faxes sent to Sarajevo using a system called System 2700? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I asked two questions, in a sense. Firstly, are you aware of Serbs intercepting faxes during the war, faxes sent to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were talking about it, but I'm not sure whether they were able to do that and whether they were doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second part of the question was System 2700. Are you aware of that system or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now turning to Srebrenica, as far as communications with Srebrenica were concerned, were you aware that for this whole period that we're discussing, Srebrenica was also under siege and completely cut off from the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness did answer "Yes". I heard her say so quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you could repeat your answer. You're aware that Srebrenica was under siege and cut off from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware that the conditions there were pretty primitive, to use a word which you used earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also aware at the time that Srebrenica communicated with the rest of the world, with Sarajevo, with Tuzla, through ham radio, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you personally didn't intercept any communications, did you, between Sefer Halilovic and anyone in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if there were to be a conversation between someone in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, would it have to go through the following route, and I'll explain -- I'll explain the route: A phone line in Sarajevo would go to the exchange; it would then be transmitted to Tuzla; and then in Tuzla, someone would have to put a phone against a ham radio -- against a radio and pick up the ham radio from Srebrenica. Do you agree that that's how a communication would be affected between Srebrenica and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the technical parts which I really cannot answer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But do you agree, based on your experience working at the SDB, that that sort of a conversation would be easily intercepted by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right, and just taking conversations between Sarajevo and Tuzla, that the quality of the conversations was very poor, indeed, and very difficult to actually listen to sometimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the connection could be lost sometimes in the middle of the conversation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just on Sefer Halilovic for a moment, he, in fact, knew, didn't he, that his line was under surveillance. To your knowledge, you're aware that he knew that he was being intercepted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the period during which the phone conversations were intercepted - I can't really remember what year it was because it was a long time ago - Mr. Sefer Halilovic was brought to our offices for interviews and he was aware of all the measures taken against him by our services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I understood your question, your previous -- your last question, Mr. Jones, to mean whether Mr. Halilovic knew that his telephone conversations were being monitored and intercepted at the time they were being intercepted? Because, if I read the witness well, he may have come to know that at some later point in time. But does she mean to tell us that at the time this interception process was taking place, Mr. Halilovic knew that his phone was bugged, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think she just answered in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could we have your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard you say "poslije," by which I understood you to mean that Mr. Sefer Halilovic learned later his telephone calls were being intercepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when he came to our office for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I wonder if the witness could be shown -- it's Prosecution Exhibit P355. I wasn't intending to use it, but it seems appropriate at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'll see in that exhibit, there's an extract -- I'm sorry, I don't have the exact reference in front of me, but it's an interception, and "Z" there says: "Telephone is being listened in by the corps." "S" for Sefer - I don't know if you can find this part of the intercept - "No it is being listened in by the MUP." Z: "By the MUP, actually?" S: "By the MUP, by the MUP. Let them listen." I have to, for myself, find the date of that intercept. But do you have that? Do you see that in the exhibit you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which page is it on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, sorry, in the English, it's page 5 of 6, and it's -- yes, P355. I apologise, P355 is, of course, one that's been used. In the B/C/S, I'm just going to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 9. Seven or eight lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see there where it says "iz MUP-a," and then "neki slusju" or something to that effect. Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you agree that from that it appears that, at any rate, on the 2nd of March, I believe it is, on the 2nd of March, 1993, Sefer Halilovic knew that he was being listened into by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You need to know, when you read something like this, all persons whose phone calls were intercepted, over all the years that I was doing this, most people, when they spoke over the phone, especially when they spoke about the things they were not supposed to talk about, they would say, Don't say too much because they're listening to, and then they would continue. So this may mean something. It may also mean nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, I want to ask you a little bit more about the equipment which you were using in your department. It's correct, isn't it, that it wasn't particularly sophisticated equipment which you were using to listen in on these conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what to say. It was the equipment we had before the war. I think it was of relatively high quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that there were two systems, one was called 12 and another system was called 64. Are either of those two systems familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right that there were only four permanent operatives for all the intercept work which was going on in 1992 or 1993, or was it that there were only four operatives that were working on the Halilovic intercept work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that. There were four of you working in your section, weren't there, four permanent staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were there, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my department, there were up to 20 people, sometimes 25 or 30. Depends on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all those people were doing the same work as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had I think what's referred to as objects, namely, the persons whose conversations were being intercepted. Is that correct, firstly, that that was the term being used, "object"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so Sefer Halilovic was an object for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had other objects as well, didn't you, whose conversations you were listening to at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not me personally, but all of us. So this was not done by one single person but by all the employees of our department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate, roughly, how many objects were being intercepted, let's say, in February 1993, by your department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say that. There were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say a hundred, more than a hundred, hundreds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Maybe some 30 or 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be more pertinent to know exactly the system that they had in place, how much or how many intercepts it could handle at any one time? Because, like in every other, there is a limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I'm seeking to establish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may wish to monitor the telephone conversations of a thousand persons, but it depends on the system that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it correct, Witness, that if you have 30 or 40 objects, each of whom is making telephone calls, possibly many telephone calls every day, that there are literally thousands of phone calls which you would be having to intercept, and that it wasn't actually possible for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you to listen to each one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I was doing that. You asked how many phone lines there were that were intercepted. There was a war on. So you are now asking a question that I simply cannot answer. The war was on. We had enemies around us. And there were many phone lines and phone calls that were the result -- and the result of them is everything that is happening here at the moment, from the Milosevic trial on. So there were many people who were working on this. We took shifts, we worked night and days. We did not go home in order to achieve the result that we did achieve eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to get clear that there's no criticism whatsoever when I talk about the system. It's really to establish that there was a huge amount of work, a huge amount of phone calls, and that by necessity, your work was selective, if not somewhat random. Would you agree with that? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think I object to that question. The witness earlier testified that she didn't know the process by which persons were targeted or, rather, selected for -- to be -- for their telephone conversations to be intercepted, or how those decisions were arrived at, and that is essentially what Mr. Jones is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not, in fact, asking about the system of choosing objects. It's once objects are chosen, the impossibility of listening to all their telephone conversations, that's the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's keep it -- MR. DI FAZIO: Then I'll withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and, in fact, I mean, because I had understood that the -- the same as you had, Mr. Di Fazio. But now the question is being limited to what has been stated by Mr. Jones, so basically let me put the question myself to you, Witness. It's being put to you that, given the large number of telephone conversations or telephone lines that needed to be tapped or monitored, there was a practical impossibility of listening, or to listen to all these telephone conversations. Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- because had Mr. Di Fazio not stood up, I was going to intervene a little bit myself. I think we need to have clarified here by the witness, in as far as how the system worked, that she, as an operative, whether she was detailed only to cover this particular person over a specified period of time, or whether she was dealing with more than, let's say, Sefer Halilovic or that particular telephone -- telephone line. Because if she was dealing with one person, obviously, the picture emerges one way; if she was dealing with more than one object, and more than one telephone line, obviously, I mean, it's the case of putting some of the questions that you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That does need clarification, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have more than one -- did you have only one object, Sefer Halilovic, or did you have more than one object in this period that we're looking at, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to try to get some more detail of actually how you worked, isn't it right that you were seated at a desk, or something of that nature, and you had a sort of switchboard in front of you and lights would go on when any of the interesting numbers were activated. Is that right, firstly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So isn't it right, then, that sometimes more than one light would go up and you would have to be selective in deciding which one you were going to listen to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I thought that the tape, the monitoring, the recording itself, was something which was automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand the recording was automatic but the listening is something which the operative would do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but let's take a system which is capable of handling 30 phones -- telephone lines at the same time. I take it that we're talking of 30 and not more than 30, and that if they all switch on together at the same time, they will all be monitored at the same time. And then it's the question of transcribing what's on tape on to paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's a matter which requires further clarification, because monitoring is -- recording is one thing; monitoring is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the recorder, you have to start with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then obviously, if she's in charge of, say, three or four objects within the same -- in the same time frame, the question that arises is whether, on any particular day, there has been recordings taken from each of these four telephone lines, whether she would transcribe the four of them or whether she would choose which ones to transcribe. I mean, that's -- and in case she had this right to choose, whether she would then transcribe the rest the following day, or how she would operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I think there's a matter even before that which needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it right that you were not only transcribing, but you were actually also listening to conversations as they occurred; and if they were of interest, notifying your supervisor of the conversation and suggesting that that conversation might be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would inform my superiors, but I wouldn't make any suggestions whatsoever. It was up to my superiors to decide what would be transcribed and what would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this is very important. In other words, the moment the switching-on mechanism in this system would go on, in other words, the moment that you know that there is a telephone -- I think there is a problem with the interpretation. Can you ... The moment that the light switches on and you, therefore, know that there is a telephone conversation which has just started on that particular telephone line that is being monitored, would you be listening in as the telephone conversation progresses, goes on, or would you listen to the conversation afterwards from the tape? This is an important question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once a conversation has ended, I take the tape off, I insert the tape into the recorder, and then I write it down. If there is something I'm not clear about, or if there's something that's in dispute, I consult with my superior and then they tell me exactly what to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So may I take over for a while?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you it's with all good intentions to try and get the right information here. So basically, you did not involve yourself in the process from the very moment that the light switched on, showing that the conversation had just started. You would come into the picture when the conversation is over. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, experience teaches that people who are using a telephone line do not discuss business all the time, every day, and on every single occasion that they are conversing. Sometimes they could be talking about cabbages, and other times they could be talking about kings. Who would make the decision or the selection of what should be left out and not transcribed, you or any one of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if it's your superiors, do I take it that, before the tape reaches you, it would have been listened to by some one else before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would listen to the tape and brief my superior on the substance of the conversation just briefly, who's taking part and what the subject matter is, based on which my superior would tell me to write the whole thing up, or just write up an abbreviated report or official note, whatever they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I put it to you that what we have here in the documents that contain your handwriting and that you saw earlier on, those three documents, that basically you wrote that because that was the part that was indicated to you by your superior for transcription.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not ask any further questions, more than that, I mean, because this is something that occurs in all trials, obviously, the editing. So I leave it up to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how busy you were, working 24 hours. We've seen on exhibits tendered today that the conversations have been reported on the same day that they were held. Now, my question is: Reporting is not the same thing as writing up the transcript, is it, firstly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But you must take into account the fact that we were professional employees and qualified to do our job. We were perfectly able to summarise conversations, take them to our superiors, and then it was up to them to decide -- to decide what we would be doing next or not. That was their decision, their call, not ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. It's just to establish this, really: That when it says that these transcripts were reported on the same day that the conversation was held, that doesn't mean you actually wrote it up that day, does it? You might have written up the conversation some time later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If a transcript states, like this one does, that the conversation took place on the 2nd of March, 1993, and that the report was submitted on the same day, then it means that both took place on the same day. It may be two or three hours later, but it was all within one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the fact that it was written up the same day for these Halilovic intercepts reflect the fact that he was considered a very high priority object, and that there was a special priority placed on those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In wartime, this applied to all objects. They needed to be dealt with as soon as possible. Once a conversation was over, if you could, you sat down to it and you wrote it up. And this applied equally, across the board, to all objects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But among the objects, weren't some considered more important than others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at the time you were intercepting -- your office was intercepting Sefer Halilovic's conversations, he was the chief of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't he? In other words, he held the highest post in the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as such, wasn't he one of the most important figures in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And didn't the SDB chief give particular priority to intercepting his conversations, to the treatment of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In wartime conditions, nothing was a priority. Nothing was prioritised. The important thing was to deal with things as quickly as possible. No names were used. You say, Person number 1. That was a mere proposal. It would usually say, Command person of security interest. That's as much as we usually received, that's myself and my colleagues, people involved in that type of work. It was only in the further course of this work that you actually got as far as the names of the people taking part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that the SDB chief actually had a feed of certain telephone lines into his own office so that he could actually personally monitor certain conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did it sometimes happen that your chief would come to you with a tape and say, This is of interest, transcribe it, that is, a tape which you hadn't taken from the machine but was actually brought to you by your chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That never happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall ever seeing that the transcribed -- the transcripts of Sefer Halilovic's conversations were kept in a safe in the SDB chief's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The moment I finish a transcript and hand it over to the chief of my department, that's as far as my commitment goes. This is the first time I've laid eyes on this particular document, ever since I originally wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you're saying you didn't see the placement of transcripts into archives, or anything like that, after you'd drawn them up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I've drawn it up, I copy it into a notebook, put it into a file, and hand it over to the head of my department. Anything that happens to it from that moment on is not something that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is this something you're aware of: That interception of telephone conversations by the SDB was regulated by law in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. It was wartime, and I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in your work, surely you've become aware of the fact that, for interception to be lawful, the SDB chief has to actually sign the appropriate authorisation? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, Your Lordship, the witness has made her position clear. She says: "I'm not familiar with that." Now, that's the same question, asking her to speak about something which she says she's not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it doesn't exclude her knowing whether the practice was that there would be an authorisation in writing from the SDB chief. If she knows, she knows; if she doesn't, she doesn't. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I don't have a problem with actual practices she saw and heard with her own senses, so to speak. But to go into -- if Mr. Jones intends to go into the issue of -- the legality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's why I made myself very clear in the beginning, before the witness entered the room, whether there were any preliminary problems that arose. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's not get into that, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones, I will not put the question myself. You can put it again. But it's a perfectly legitimate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the question is simply that: Are you aware that the practice was that there would be an authorisation in writing from the SDB chief in order for there to be interception of telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've told you, what we received is a proposal. Then it would seem logical that this proposal has been approved. Whether there was an actual authorisation or not is far above my head. This is all I do. Everything that is above that station is not something that I used to deal with. I did receive a proposal every single time, I did and so did my colleagues. A measure has been exposed -- has been imposed for security reasons against such and such a person, that was usually stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you're saying that, in relation to Sefer Halilovic, you saw such a proposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She didn't say that the proposal was in writing, so I suppose you'll ask that question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the proposal usually be in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, typewritten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see a typewritten proposal in relation to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you saw that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it the moment the phone line was about to be established, or rather, the tapping of a certain phone line. So just before that occurs, a proposal comes along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up, Mr. Jones. The proposal would not mention the name of the person, it would mention his -- it would just mention an object and a pseudonym referring to that object and not his name, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending. Sometimes it was a pseudonym; sometimes it was with the full name -- first name and last name stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the case of Sefer Halilovic, are you saying that you saw his full name on a proposal, before the interception started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It said "Command." That's all it said. "Measure imposed against" such and such a phone number, headquarters, and then the code name given later was Skup, S-k-u-p. And then once you start processing this, you get to hear who the actual persons are, and then you realise it's Sefer Halilovic, once you've heard it 10 or 15 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But did Skup refer to the command -- the phone -- the command of the Bosnian army or refer to Sefer Halilovic personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a question that I can't answer. My job was to write it down, which I did. Now, what that was in reference to, I really can't say. One thing you must understand is that this is my job, and what I do, I take the tape off, I write down the conversation, I consult my superior on what should be done next. Everything that comes before or after is something that I simply don't do and something that I'm simply not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine, and that's clear. But just to clarify this, then: Before -- the first intercept we've seen dates from the 11th of February, 1993. So is it your evidence that before that date, you saw a typewritten proposal referring to Skup and the command, monitoring telephone conversations on that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But when you receive a proposal, you have no idea what it's about. It's none of your business. You receive a proposal. You see that it's something that is of security interest. This is just for you, for your intuition as an operative officer to know that this is about security or about a military matter. It doesn't matter whether it's something negative or something positive. You just write it down, because that's what your superior wants you to do. And it's only through your actual work that you find out the actual substance of what's going on on an actual phone line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. But are you given - just to follow up on that - given instructions as to what to look for in particular as the process of intercepting goes on, from your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I've just told you, isn't it? It really depends on who you're talking about specifically. He usually specifies everything that's military. If they're talking about military operations, sometimes if you're not certain, you have to go back and ask them. If there's a conversation and you're not sure about what you should write down and what you shouldn't, then you go back to your boss and you confer in order to clarify matters. If you tell him, for example, there's a man on this line talking about this and that, then he may as well tell you, Write down the whole thing. It wasn't my job to decide what I would write down. The actual writing was my job, but nothing else. I'm not going into the terminology, who's calling or who specifically they're calling. My job is to listen to the tape and write down whatever they say I should.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. Now, isn't it correct that every audiotape which is transcribed is generally preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, though, that for the audiotapes of the intercepts that you've transcribed, which we've seen today, that they have not been preserved? Is that something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, we would like to pass up an exhibit. The ERN number is 03618459 to 03618460. There's one minor correction, in fact, to the English. On page 2, item 13, the number under May 10, 1993 should be "797-7299".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you, Witness, to look at items 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Before we proceed, this document must not be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would look at items 7, 8, and 9 on page 1, and then 13, those, I suggest, are the intercepts which we've looked at. And isn't it right that for three of them, it's written there that there is no audio, and for the fourth one, there's only an unusable stored audio recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I've heard of it. I really can't say. I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this before the break - I see the time: You worked in the SDB, under different names, for more than 20 years. Based on your experience, do you find it extraordinary that these tapes have not been preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's extraordinary, especially the transcripts got this far and suddenly there's no audio recording. Why? Who knows. I did my job, and this was down to some other persons. Why this came about, I really can't say. I can't answer a question that I'm not familiar with. All I can say is that, during the war, we had difficulties with tapes, with stationery, with pens and pencils. We had nothing at all. Everything was in short supply, so sometimes tapes were erased to make space for something else to be recorded. This is a just a thought occurring to me right now. But I really can't say why there is no audio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would just ask that this document be given a Defence exhibit number, and then we can have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know the sequence. This would be Defence Exhibit D?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 204. And it will be entered and kept under seal, please. We'll have a break now. In the meantime, because this should be a follow-up to your question and her answer, perhaps she could enlighten us whether there was a system of copying these cassettes on to reels, big reels, because that's usually how it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. During the break, I've reviewed my questions. I have literally three remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. We certainly do not have that problem today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, that's for sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, firstly, just following up on a matter raised by His Honour before the break concerning whether there was a system for copying audiotapes onto reel-to-reel tapes, I propose to read a paragraph from a prior statement which you appear to have given to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 5th of July, 2004, and you can simply tell me if it's correct or not. And it's paragraph 13 from that statement. It says there: "Every audiotape which is transcribed will be preserved. It may not be the same tape that was recorded, but it will be copied to big tapes (reel-to-reel) if the recordings are in small portions. I do not know and when this process took place.
