However, all the records which are transcribed will be kept in safe custody." Could can you confirm? Yes, if you could repeat that, please. Could you confirm that that's the correct position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now two final questions: The surveillance of Sefer Halilovic's telephone was conducted over many months, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate approximately how many months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly, but certainly two or three months. Maybe even more, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that period, surveillance was 24 hours a day, wasn't it, either by you or one of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. It was done by me and many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was 24-hours-a-day surveillance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours a day, except for the times when we had no electricity, no power, no generator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you personally did not intercept any conversation between Sefer Halilovic and anyone in Srebrenica during that whole period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, is there re-examination? MR. DI FAZIO: Just one question arising out of that last one or two questions that you were just asked now. Re-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a telephone call came in to the phone that you were targeting and recording, did you know where the incoming call originated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that if the caller was known to me, or if, during the conversation, the caller identified himself, otherwise, I could not know unless identified during the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser would like to -- Judge Eser is going to put some questions to you, madam. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have just one question for clarification, for translation. There have been some discussion on the documents where it is said that a conversation was reported. That was today. Now, in the English translation, sometimes that was translated as transcribed, drawn up, and so on. And what I wanted to know, and also with the help of the interpreters, what does it mean -- if I draw your attention to document P354, do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think she has. Don't answer. She doesn't have it so let's give it to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, my question is: If you go on the first page, where you have these statements regarding the 11th of February, 1993, the last line I'm not familiar with your language, now, what does that mean? Would it be correct to translate it as "reported," or does it mean something else? The question is also put to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conversation held, this means that the conversation was held on the 11th of February, 1993, and then reported on the same day. So this is the report, the report or transcript. I consider that to be one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These recordings, these tapes, were they being kept, stored, in the same building where the tapping was taking place, or were they being stored in some other building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were kept in the same building. I'm not sure where exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was this the only building from which tapping, telephone tapping, was taking place, or was there some other place where it was taking place as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware only of this building in which I also worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does this building still exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it was never destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not aware of any other building that was being used for tapping that was destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, which basically means that your testimony comes to an end here, which also means that Madam Usher will now escort you. We will -- I don't think we need to go into private session in this room to -- while she is leaving the courtroom. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't think we need to go into private session while she leaves the courtroom. Madam, on behalf of the Tribunal, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, also on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, I should like to thank you for coming over to give testimony in this case. You will be escorted, and you're free to go back to your country. On behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one matter which is just -- and perhaps I should have mentioned it as a preliminary, but it's this: That we haven't challenged the authenticity of these four exhibits, P354, P355, P356, and P360, but there are questions of authorisation with regard to the intercepts which I was asking about during the course of this witness' testimony, and Your Honour devined the reason for that. We would like to do is reserve our position on this for the time being, because my understanding is that in the Halilovic trial, the Defence will almost certainly raise challenges of that nature and we wanted to preserve our position until the Trial Chamber has given its ruling on that matter. It's -- obviously, they are different proceedings, but at the same time, in the interests of -- in the interests of harmony, if the Trial Chamber in Halilovic were to take a certain position with regard to the legality or otherwise of the intercepts, and the consequences of any ill legality, we of course would want to be able to make submissions in that regard. So it's simply to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Basically, I will not say much, because I am neither the Prosecutor nor the Defence. But basically this matter was, as you hinted earlier on, regulated by the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, the Trial Chamber will decide in accordance to what is before it and not in accordance to what it may have learnt from other experiences and other cases. But just to put you in the picture, there was a law in place before the war broke out whereby authorisation had -- there was a chain specified as to where authorisation to intercept telephone conversations could originate from. And in the other cases that I am aware of, the document authorising the intercept and describing also the object, and giving him or her the nom de plume exists, I don't know whether it exists in this case, obviously, it's beyond my knowledge, then after -- before the war you know there was the Presidency composed of all the ethnicities. The situation changed after the beginning of the war, but the matter was regulated after the beginning of the war as well by an ad hoc provision. So the question of legality did arise. It arose in the Brdjanin case, it arose also in the Milosevic case in relation to admissibility, the same in Brdjanin, so there are similar sources you can have access to. But in some other cases, we have had persons who were or are still in the employ of the agency, AID, and what came after it and what was before it, who were in a very good position to provide all the information. Also, with regard to the chain of custody of these reels -- but anyway, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I think I'm just trying to help both of you out by giving you information that I know of. Of course, I will obliterate all this information from my mind, as far as this case is concerned, unless I have evidence which relates precisely to these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I can tell you that, letters of authorisation signed by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, president of the Presidency, do exist, letters of authorisation signed by the minister for home affairs or internal affairs do exist, and they have been exhibited in other cases. But what exists in this particular case as regards Halilovic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour. I believe actually the matter hasn't been fully litigated yet, but, of course, I'm aware that in many cases Rule 95 arguments have been raised in relation to intercept evidence, and human rights arguments based on Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the right to privacy, et cetera. So it's really to anticipate possibly piggybacking, if I can put it that way, on Halilovic Defence submissions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, the question of legality was debated at the Brdjanin case, but the period of time to which it related is somewhat different, because it related to the period of time when -- this is the early period, even preceding the war, even preceding the war, where members of the Presidency were tapping telephones of other members of the Presidency as well. But in any case, so there might not be a parallel on which to argue that. But the question of legality did -- obviously was argued, but I don't think those arguments would fit in this particular case, because now we're talking of 1993, definitely, and the picture had changed by then as far as the law, applicable law, is concerned, if I remember well. But again, until and unless these matters are brought to the attention of this particular Trial Chamber, you can rest assured that this is the beginning and the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. To use a phrase of Your Honours, those may be pleasures that await us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pleasures yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Pleasures yet to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pleasures yet to come, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I've heard everything, and there's nothing much that I can add to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. MR. DI FAZIO: Just one thing, if I may say this: I've got no problem with the Defence reserving their position, but I don't know what the schedule is for any decision-making on a similar issue in the Halilovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either. MR. DI FAZIO: No. And the scenario that I would not like to see develop is this argument being launched at the end of the Prosecution case, when we're not in a position to address it with further evidence or to assist you on the topic. And so, whereas I say there's no problem, of course, with Mr. Jones reserving his position, at some point or another, I think he will have to inform us whether he's going to run this argument or not, because at the moment the tapes are in evidence and they're before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, I mean, this is -- what I'm coming to is a provision that -- you may like it or you may not like it, but I usually try not to apply much. But it is there. I'll soon come to it, please. Leave it for the time being, because we're going to waste time on this. I thought it was 80 -- anyway, leave it. I will tell you at some future point in time, but it's a question of what should be raised during cross-examination and what could not be raised at a future point in time if it has not been contested to the witness during the cross-examination. But I am -- I can't see it at the moment. So it's an important provision which has been borrowed from the English current practice, which was applied very strictly in some other instances which can cause problems. But anyway, let's not waste time on it. I think I've said enough. Point taken. Point taken, and that's it. And in any case, I don't think that this was the witness which could be faced with the question of authenticity in any case, because she was only familiar with some information but not with all, as often happens in such organisations as the one she works in, or used to work it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I did put the matter to her, though, for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what's more important is this: That I was given the impression, and when I say "I," I mean the three of us here, we were given the impression that this witness would last here in the witness box today and tomorrow. Now we've finished with her, and of course I'm going to look at you straight in the eyes, Mr. Wubben, so that you tell me what's going to happen tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the next witness been proofed or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The next witness is in the stage of proofing, also tomorrow morning, and looking at the developments of today, we anticipated, indeed, that we should start tomorrow. But to what extent, I also made a kind of assessment. We are -- we think and we project that we might need the beginning of the afternoon, so if it's possible to start at -- after the first break, we should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suggest you do what we do in my country with jurors when we come to the final stages: We don't let them go and have a proper meal, lunch, we provide them with sandwiches, and they continue working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's also a matter, Your Honour, of course, of the proofing notes and the rest for the witness himself to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I'm sure that, Mr. Wubben, knowing you that, that you will do your level best. Who is proofing this witness, yourself or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please do convey the message that it is our wish that we try and do our best to start at 2:15 as scheduled. Of course, if that is not possible, we will start later. But I do appreciate your efforts to make sure that we can at least continue tomorrow and not miss or waste a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will start, indeed, with that full intention, and we will update -- I will update further senior legal officer, or legal officer, in that respect, whenever it becomes clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Please, rest assured that the three of us will be at your disposal here, ready to start at 2.15, if that's the case. And we'll probably be here in the morning too. So any communication that you need to place or effect will arrive and will be tackled, dealt with, straight away, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we can -- is there anything else? Any further business?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it might be Rule 90(H)(ii) which Your Honour was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I couldn't remember -- I was there but I was wasting more time. Yes, that's it. So let's adjourn for today. We'll reconvene tomorrow at 2.15, with the saving that we mentioned earlier. Thanks.
